Working at an Amazon Fullfillment Center is unpredictable. The medical insurance is the reason most people stay at Amazon. It’s high quality and inexpensive and starts on day 1. Remember the board game Life? So many opportunities to be successful and then you draw a card and your success starts to fall apart. That’s how success is at Amazon for both men and women. It does seem that when women move up in the company they seem to have more job security than the men. However, to move up, you must be cutthroat. For both men and women in all departments and levels, making family a priority is highly looked down upon, which makes single mothers/fathers have to fight many battles to keep their jobs especially with their strict attendance policies. Furthermore, most employees have had to experience worker’s comp within their 2 years of working there and struggle to return to work if it was a bad injury such as in the spine, shoulder, etc. The maternity leave is amazing and it’s all paid for mothers and fathers. The shifts are 10 hours which gives you 3 days off each week, although at least 1 of those days will be used to recover physically or sleep. Overtime is wonderful when it’s voluntary but during peak seasons or when attendance/staffing is low mandatory overtime is started and they’ll only have to give notice before 4pm the previous day. Fortunately they only allow up to 60 hours per week because they push it to the minute during peaks. That’s six 10 hour physically intense, rate driven days per week during summer and the holidays. If you needed that time off that they’ve called mandatory overtime, you must use your allotted paid or unpaid time off. When you go below that amount, you’ve broken the attendance policy and are up for termination. You can go to HR and try to get it excused, but that’s a hit or miss. Sometimes they can’t do much for you but if approved you can take an medical leave minimum of 7 days if it’s a medical reason, possibly a personal leave minimum of 15 days if it’s not (only medical during peak unless it’s an extreme case with documentation). So, there are options, but they aren’t easy nor are they a sure deal.

Equal pay and opportunity. Minimum company wage is $15 an hour to start with benefits and vacation days. Some room for advancement. BUT be prepared for long hours. Part time is also available but I'm not sure what those shift options would be. You'll be on your feet all day, I did get use to it after a couple weeks. Medical benefits are great and they work with a ton of other companies that you can get discounts through, including disney tickets but they have so much more. I can't say it is the most satisfying job I have ever done as I'm not doing something I enjoy or saw myself doing, but the pay is good and my coworkers are super nice. Opportunity for extra time occasionally. Opportunity for voluntary time off where you can accept time off for the day if they know it isn't going to be busy, and it will not use your vacation time, you just have the day off without pay and it doesn't count against you. Which is great especially if you have a side job. Cafeteria plays movies and has game tables. Food vendors come during lunch hours, or they have their own little "grocery store" with food you can buy for lunch. Refrigerators to store lunch, plenty of microwaves and utensils. After working there a year, they have a school program where they will pay 95% of tuition for certain programs. One I'm interested in is to do ultrasound, but they have others. So you can make good money if you don't mind the strain on your body and working 50 hours a week.  My body hurt so bad that I couldn't even sleep when I would get home and my feet would swell up for days.  This job might be okay for someone in their 20's who wants to keep up with it and get promoted because it did seem like they promoted people pretty quickly if they do a good job.
Very equal opportunity in all aspects
Interacting with people is such a great stress reliever!

Amazon's time off system is extremely flawed, and sets employees (especially parents with special needs children) up for failure. You only get set hours of unpaid time off, anything over that has to be earned by working overtime. Of you have no more time off, emergency or not, you are penalized. This is unfair to parents caring for disable or special needs children that may have to miss work to care for an I'll child. You are forced to risk losing your job regardless of performance if you have to miss work and don't have unpaid time to cover it.
My direct manager admitted to me that he can't deal with women. He was telling a coworker and i to stop whining about things that are going wrong and need to be addressed by him.
I loved working at Amazon. There were so many amenities and the people were great and supportive.
It took an older male confidant to convince my three younger to middle-aged male managers to respect what I had to say when I repestedly expressed a bullying issue in my department.

Amazon is a quick paced work environment, once you have that mastered, promotion is achievable. A major challenge is the ability to move from one branch of the industry (production/ factory manager) to another branch of the company (subsidiary branch). Consistent networking connections can help in making transitions a little bit simpler, but it is a difficult process.
I've had a lot of jobs in my life and I can sincerely say that Amazon is the most employee-friendly company that I've worked with.

Very unorganized, not open to new ideas, not professional, and lots of he said she said. When the warehouse first opened it was very warm and management was great, then it went down hill, you could tell they hated their jobs.

Amazon is the epitome of white male privilege. amazon have great intentions towards providing a diverse workplace, but in reality do not.  Women , specifically those in the creative field, are bypassed for promotions, denigrated, demeaned and ignored.
Females are well respected but they seem to have a harder time with promotions.
Your happiness is heavily dependent upon your organization.
Amazon is a hard place to work for

I have found my experience to be demoralizing because I came in with ambition, big goals, and bought in to the endless opportunity Amazon markets to candidates. My experience has been very different from what was sold to me from recruiters to hiring managers. Amazon is very classist, if you are not in a senior role then you're labeled as ineffective. New opportunities are in high demand and hard to come by.  If you are not careful (treat everyday like you are on thin ice) then your peers and leadership will discredit you until you ultimately leave the company. The turnover rate is kept hush-hush for good reason, we can't keep intelligent people for very long.

Amazon is better than a lot of places I have worked. However, being the wealthiest company in the world,  you would think they could afford to pay people more, provide better insurance,have more sick time and provide wellness and childcare programs.

Hugely unorganized. The work, benefits are good, but they overwork everyone. Mandatory OT for weeks on end. Management tends to be cliquey and let friends get away with things anyone else would be immediately fired for. (playing on the internet or socializing during and entire shift or even sleeping during a shift)
I have had many fantastic opportunities at Amazon, and I love the flexibility that I have to be with my family when needed.
Women in all levels of management. Mothers Room for privacy. Equal pay. Free feminine products in the ladies room.
Dd
They work you to the bone then fire you when you cant keep up anymore.

Most promotions go to men. And the women management that they do have, they cycle them out faster than most (excluding hr). And if the management doesn't like you then your ass good as gone. They'll harass you until you quit.
They try to promote females but fail. The ones they have high up give us a bad reputation.

You're allowed 18 minutes "off task" in your ten hour shift to go to the bathroom, and if you're on a conveyor position, you'll have to hit an alarm and then wait for a manager to cover your station before you're allowed to go. 99% of the time this manager will be male and will make you feel awkward for asking to go more than twice a day. They'll also ALWAYS send a male manager to "address going over your time off task quota" aka scold you for needing to go to the bathroom. It might be less of an issue if we had more than 2 30 minute breaks for the whole ten hour day, and if walking to and from break took less than five minutes each way.

I'm sure someone else has gone into depth about the huge problem Amazon has with underreporting repetitive motion injuries and their vastly disproportionate young white male majority in leadership- but this is not that write up. I'm here to solely to warn you, if you don't like having your bathroom habits monitored and controlled, this is definitely a hellish workplace. If you suffer from PMDD or even just a generally awful period, seriously don't subject yourself to this.

Overall, I do not mind my job. However, it always seems that there are far less women in higher positions. On top of that, sexual harassment by coworkers is often rampant and it does not seem that much is done about it. In my own personal experiences, hardly anything was done about the coworkers I reported for sexual harassment. These are my two biggest concerns with my job.

It was openly supported to treat women differently,  to talk over them in meetings,  to have a totally different grading scale for work.  If a man wanted your project or job,  they would accuse  women of 'being emotional'  because they couldn't find fault in the work and that was good enough to have a woman removed from the position.  Men took credit for others work and you were never allowed to use facts against a man in a meeting.
Very physically demanding job. Has good days and bad.

Amazon has a lot to offer if you're willing to give your life to your work. I was working 60 to 70 hour work weeks and then was told I need to work more. There are opportunities for advancement but it's all about the people you know.
Amazon does not do as good a job of using data to drive decision-making about employee support as it could.

AWS is as bad as you read in the New York Times. I only stayed a year and have taken an executive position in another major tech company. I have almost 20 years experience and AWS was awful. Not recommended especially for women. They're years behind in diversity and tolerate behavior other employers would fire employees for immediately. It was appalling.  It's hostile and women are treated like admins regardless of their expertise and experience.
I am unreasonably happy in my job.  I work with strong women leaders and I have great opportunities to learn from them.
Amazon does not seem to value is employees. I left because I quickly learned I had little chance of being promoted. I would never work there again.
I feel like it is time we are honest when someone, especially a big business, gets it right. Amazin gets it right in a big way.
Amazon has its ups and downs but is definitely a good workplace that is always moving forward in positive ways, I'm happy to be a woman working for this company

I am a recruiter with in the tech department. I am run ragged on a daily basis. I was not properly trained yet when given a chance to be trained we were forced to work while in the training. I have a brain/memory disorder that requires me to work harder than the average person to absorb new information/processes. I asked if it would be possible to work from home every now and then so that the stress from the daunting office day to day won't interfere with my learning process. When I did this I was told that if I had the will to learn I would find a way! I am currently in the process of looking for a new job at a new company!
Great benefits, excellent parental leave, great people to work with very diverse. Not a lot of women in leadership roles though

There are no females in senior management.  There are currently less women in management on the floor than I have fingers on my left hand. Tampon dispensers are always empty. Bathrooms are nasty. Men are not held accountable for sexual harassment in my experience whether it was physical or verbal. The benefits for maternity are amazing but LOA team makes it near impossible to get these benefits by not returning calls and giving you the run around and not answering you. There is no on-site representation so everything has to be done via phone and during their work hours; which does not match up with many of MKE1 full-time shifts.

Though the workforce is fairly even and lower management levels have pretty even levels of female equivalents the higher managers seem to be primarily male.  Parental leave and personal paid and unpaid time as well as vacation are great perks along with healthcare that make it easier to have a family and work here

I was told I was not chummy enough with fellow managers (all male, discussed only sports) given poor review based on feelings, contrary to performance metrics. Took a leave of absence which was treated with disdain by hr and Sr mgmt. Was told management did not use personal time for illness, or only when "legitimately sick" without any knowledge of my illness.

My main issue is the policy of time off task wich covers bathroom breaks.  Certain positions make it almost 100% sure that you'll be far away from a bathroom with only a 5 minute window to get there use the bathroom and back before time is counting against you.

Working at Amazon you are expected to work all the time. If you get an email or phone call at 2am, you are expected to reply at 2am. You are never off. Ever. You will work with the smartest people you have ever known. You will learn more than you ever have. And after a year or two, you will be more exhausted than you have ever been. It is not uncommon to see men and women crying at their desks and in the hallways.
I love amazon and have been learning so much. It's one of those jobs if you do it for a long time you can be amazing or you can move up.
Amazon is actually very fair.  I've moved up,  there are a good amount of female leaders,  though my building is mostly males.

Amazon is very progressive and very diverse. Women get free tampons and pads, the ratio of women to men management is the best I've seen at any job, and there is a very inclusive environment. Enjoyable working environment and HR cares about the employees

I was sexually harassed almost daily and a lot of males seemed to have my back, but mainly because they thought I was cute or wanted to have sex with me. It also seemed to be a male dominated environment, so I suppose that could have been part of it.

Second Full filament center I've worked at...love a company that as a female even provides hygiene products without feeling the need to charge us for them. It's the little things that sometimes make the biggest difference.

On the outside, it looks progressive. On the inside, associates and power leadership are thorns in the side. It's so hard to get meetings with upper management. They have no time to work with you on your development. It's so sad.

Amazon is an amazing company to work for!  The pay, benefits and accommodations for all scenarios are outstanding. From my father's death to my own health issues, they have always gone above and beyond to assist however they can. They also encourage furthering education,  and pay 95% after one year. I could go on and on about all that they provide for employees!
We aren't offered anything and if you don't measure up you're gone. Not allowed to talk about it. It's forbidden.

Although it is not the horrible company that a lot of reviews state, there is still much room for improvement. If a salaried manager is working 13 hour days instead of 10, do not get upset when they go home early for being sick once in awhile, or quickly ask if they put in their time for it. Salaried managers usually give much time at work plus time at home working from their computers to assist the company in its growth. Conduct thorough reviews on your Sr Management team to ensure they do not play favorites at sites, which can cause low morale and unneeded drama. Lastly, create a better on-boarding for the college hires that become managers. Some of these students have never worked a day in their life and they are now in charge of 50+ people. In order for them and the company to be successful provide tracked training site specific.
Always considerate and understanding

Women are often excluded from conversations, or when they are present, things are not said. Even in management, women are given less projects and analytical expectations, yet are held to higher standards of professional conduct, especially when handling their emotions. When a woman is doing anything other than smiling or agreeing, if she is lucky enough to even be heard, she is told to step back and evaluate how she's speaking or portraying her face for the sake of her OLR. It's your good old fashioned boys' club, with a powerful modern nuance.

I've experienced that I'm paid less than my male counter parts at every level in the company I've worked. Same job, same years of experience, less pay. Cannot receive a merit increase except for at specific times of the year and if granted, it's the same as everyone's so even if a raise is provided, my male colleagues get the same raise, never decreasing the wage gap.

Male management is actively dismissive of female management. Getting your voice heard in meetings is agony. My male counterparts have less experience and education than I do and make more money than I do -- their total compensation is higher. Other female managers have mentioned in private that they have discovered the same issue at their own buildings. And yes, I have spoken in specifics with my male colleagues about our total compensation packages - down to RSU vesting schedules. Male managers who excel are promoted aggressively. Female managers who excel are kept in their positions because they're "too valuable."

Amazon belittles and humiliated those to work hard, are successful and can achieve greatness for the overall well-being of the company. Providing input and suggestions isn't welcome and proposing higher positions for the same work is looked down upon. Getting demoted and eventually fired because of continued determination for the success of you and your peers is a very real possibility. Amazon does not acknowledge their own mistakes, but instead blames those who work hard daily to provide for the company, and especially if you make calls to ethics and report your managers for being ethically challenged and sexist, racist, egotistical "leaders".

They need a culture of Emotional IQ. The Indian men are the worst offenders  and tech leadership is crawling with them. Horrible unconscious bias. The worst in 20 years of being in the industry. Even the women are biased towards other women. I can't wait to find another job, but the pay chains me there till I find one and at my level it takes a while.

Great for someone wanting to get their foot in the door with a large company. A ton of room to move up if you're willing to wait. BUT Management changes often and you are more of a number than a person.
Amazon has men and women in the same positions. They are paid the same. Amazon also supplies feminine hygiene products (pads and tampons) in all bathrooms for free.

The place runs on testosterone, adversity and being 'frugal'. It is not uncommon to see internal threads about why it is unfair for the company to be offering medical benefits for new moms (and very recently dads), when people who choose not to have kids don't anything comparable. No wonder the only female Jeff B technical advisor (TA) had to be way overqualified for the job, (CEO of Quidsi vs director-level for most men chosen for the job) and was chosen 20 years into the company's existence. For those who don't know, this TA position is basically the way high potential talent gets groomed for positions like VP. She was already at a CEO level.

Though Amazon has improved  maternal and paternal leave, it is not an environment friendly to family life or work life balance. The hours pace and general base level requirements make it difficult to take any sort of time off.
Free feminine products in the restroom. Access to free pain relievers, although not a women specific product it's certainly helpful. The facility also has a lactation room.

A great place to work! Professional, fun and respectful culture. Positive managers who really care about everyone as they reach targeted goals. The focus is not just on the client, which is well known with Amazon, but also the employee needs as well through flexible schedules, a fair wage, excellent benefits, great training, a nursing room for lactating mothers, break rooms that offer offer free food, water, coffee, games and a widescreen tv. Everyone is treated with respect and there is even a computer room that employees can use at break and lunch to search for other positions! Equal opportunities are evident here. Love working for Amazon!
It's a great place to work if you are in the right role. I only wish we valued employee time more, and worked to leverage them for the roles they are hired for

Current ops admin for a new site. My knowledge of the benefits the company provides leads me to believe that this company is absolutely a great place for women and parents in general to work. I work long hours but only 4 days a week and the pay I receive is absolutely competitive.
You should ask about work-life balance company can have good terms but make you work a lot this does not enable to grow your family.

Blown away by the lactation room (complete with relatively comfortable chair, fridge, sink, and soap) and the level of support given to those of us who were nursing mothers. I was unprepared for such positivity. During those long nights of picking, pumping became my favorite part of the work day. It was so appreciated.
They hire managers straight out of college and that needs to be worked on some more. Some managerial experience should be required for such a big place.
Big old boys club. Upper leaders take credit for other's work when it succeeds, she'd blame on to others for their own mistakes.
Upper management is mostly men. Dock positions are all men, even if women prove themselves

I was a work from home employee. I enjoyed most aspects of my job and the maternity leave was to die for. Seriously no one does maternity better than Amazon.  I took a buyout and left. The program needs work but it's headed in the right direction. Amazon is innovative and will always thrive. I hope, because I still love them dearly. 

    _sandshol
It is what it is, then some

Don't work at a warehouse unless you're built like an Icelandic muscle head. Was given an RMI to fill out and no doctors would touch it. Was told it could be taken to an urgent care facility but that was a lie. When I did finally get it turned in, it wasn't enough and they wanted more. Doctor put restrictions on me that amazon didn't like, so they told me to either get better or leave. Underpaid, overworked, Amazon treats their employees like they're disposable, at least in states with lenient labor laws.

In general, a great company to work for. However, it's very hard for women to get promoted. Looking at my site, less than a quarter of leadership and above are women. It's definitely a boys club at Amazon.

This is based on the Redlands warehouse, horrible management all around and don't want you to succeed. A lot of favoritism and phonys. Bully you anytime you get even remotely hurt and tell you you're crazy when you say how you feel. Great company, HORRIBLE location.

When you are treated like a number instead of a human being, you feel like you are not valuable to the company in which you work. Unfortunately this has been the case for quite some time with my current place of employment. It gets exhausting to keep dealing with the same untrustworthy leadership day in and day out. Upper leadership does not seem to care, but yet they want to know why the good employees continue to leave. Until there is a significant change in leadership, people will continue to feel the same way.

In the mobile device space, there were around industry average proportion of women (not enough), but all women were in QA roles, no women in development roles. It was like the software equivalent of traditional gender roles, women were cleaning up the mess the men made. There were some few women in the management chain, but again only on the QA side.
Read the NYT article
I once complained about a female coworker who I felt was picking on me to my manager.  He told me that my coworker had higher standards for me because we were both female.
The few women in management were not right for the job (picked because they were in departments with poor performers).  Male co-workers made much more money in the same position.

When you are going through all of the new hire training, it seems as if they really care about their employees. They even have a safety team on site if anything should go wrong. However, the actual most important thing to them is productivity. I am pregnant and I can only move so fast and I need to use the restroom more often. There was no way to adjust my goals so that I could meet them and I was chastised for being pregnant in the first place.

Overall there are worse places to be a woman.  Depending on the specific team and org you're in, it can definitely be better and worse. Those orgs which have clear, written goals for diversity tend to follow through on those, so seek those out. So far, any outright harassment or discriminatory behavior is readily squashed by HR, so usually all you have to battle with is the unconscious bias and subtle sidelining. Choosing your team wisely can mitigate the unconscious bias factors.

Amazon Fulfillment Centers are very hard on managers for hours.  There is very little work-life balance and you are expected to work 60 hour weeks minimal.  I personally had core hours (hours I had to be at the facility every week) of 55 hours, but as a manager I was required to be there before the start of the shift and so I worked more than 60 every week.  When it cam time for me to take the shift that required fewer hours my male counterpart appealed to my manager that he had kids and I did not, and therefore our rotation (we were supposed to do this every 3-4 months) was stopped.

During my time there, men stating they had childhood duties were smiled upon.  I said I needed to go to visit my very ill father and our boss told me that he needed for me to turn in an assignment that Saturday by noon.  I had to stay up all night and work dutifully until noon to complete it. a document by noon.  A male co-worker stated that he needed to spend time with his kids a few weekends later and our boss stated that life had to have those types of enjoyment.  The very next week I was asked to do what that employee failed to do the prior week.  My boss saw himself in my co-worker, there-fore he felt guilty when my male co-workers needed time with their families.  For women he just couldn't relate.   

In another case, a female co-worker made the comment that she was having childcare issues and her manager questioned whether she was cut out for the job.  

I am bringing up personal cases so it may seem like this would not apply to you.  But, Amazon is so "young" male dominated, they don't question that they aren't tolerant to different people.  They expect a homogeneous thought process and are very intolerant to people that don't share life experience.

As an entry level associate, there is no discrimination against women. They are all treated the same and get great benefits. As for moving up in the company. it is not likely for women at Amazon. There are a few supervisors that are women, but when it comes to management, from what I've seen at my buidling, only about 10% of management are women. In my 4 year career with Amazon I have never seen a woman as an Operations Manager, Senior Operations Manager, or General Manager.

Recent changes in parental / maternity leave are very positive.  Travel expectations for some roles are really challenging.  The company does not do "remote work" very well.  There's still very much a strong preference for everyone to be in Seattle.   Long hours and high expectations but manageable with the right boss, and salary is commensurate with effort in my opinion, which makes it worthwhile.  I really like my job and working for Amazon, but it is challenging, for sure.  I would be happier if there were more options for remote employees to be truly remote and unencumbered by working outside of corporate HQ.
Work life balance is non existent. Only a handful of women at the Herndon office. And several have had really awful experiences.

There seem to be more men managing team on the production floor, but the HR team has a female majority, and the sexual harassment policy is one of no tolerance. I know that if someone is exhibiting inappropriate behavior, I can bring it to someone's attention and be taken seriously.
If you are not an overgrown frat boy, you will not be promoted.  That said, Seattle is an amazing place and many people fall in love with the area and cannot bear to leave, myself included.

I've found the warehouse I work for with Amazon.com is an amazing opportunity for women AND men of all ages, races, sexual orientations, etc.  It is the most diverse workplace I've ever been in. While I'm currently in a position that has extreme potential, I find it has more options than when I was in positions of management for other companies I've worked for where I was close to the top, yet somehow still stifled with my power.  I cannot speak more highly of Amazon as a work environment that everyone could be comfortable working for.

If you're a young, single woman (or young looking) - you can do very well at Amazon. but expect your relationships to be difficult, and suffer immensely if you have children. Some managers are supportive, but many preach support then ding you in the annual review.

Women left out of critical meetings. Manager and team leads don't help with on boarding process. Quick to criticize. Micromanagement. Managers want to look good and blame employees for mistakes before trying to understand the problems. Unforgiving environment. Men posture and dominate meetings. Shouting louder gets you heard. Quick to make judgments about people.

For retail jobs:
Hours relatively inflexible due to nature of ecommerce. Work life balance is tough if you want to have career advancement. Many leave retail to start family.

Decent representation of women in retail management team. Career advancement is completely merit based which is great. Mentorship and focus on women issues is lacking.
Our President and COO is one of the most inspirational women leaders I have met.  We have a Women in Technology group that meets regularly and is supported by management.

Amazon is full of type A folks that work hard and play hard.  You can have flexibility and work-life balance but you have to figure that out on your own.  Its a great place to work if you desire freedom to do whatever you need for your role without a lot of bureaucracy.  Amazon has a way to go to get more women into leadership and technical roles.

Bro-y young tech/sales environment with grind mentality. Little to no maternity/paternity leave. Did have pretax flexible dependent FSA account to help offset child care cost which was helpful. I lucked out and had a great boss that was flexible with telecommuting if my child or self was sick. Doesn't offer part time telecommute positions to retain talented individuals who need a more flexible job while rearing small children. Very few women in non-sales aspects of company.
